questions.question_html:
Consider the following statements:
Statement I: If A is a non-singular matrix, then $A^{-1}$ exists.
Statement II: If A and B are symmetric matrices of same order, then $(AB-BA)$ is a skew symmetric matrix.
Choose the correct option.

options.label: A
options.text: Statement I is true and Statement II is false
options.html: Statement I is true and Statement II is false

options.label: B
options.text: Statement I is false and Statement II is false
options.html: Statement I is false and Statement II is false

options.html: Statement I is true and Statement II is true

options.text: Statement I is false and Statement II is true
options.html: Statement I is false and Statement II is true

questions.explanation_text: Statement I is true. A matrix $A$ is called non-singular when its determinant is not zero, that is, $|A| \ne 0$ For such a matrix, the inverse $A^{-1}$ exists. So Statement I is correct. Statement II is also true. Given that $A$ and $B$ are symmetric matrices, we have $A^{T}=A\text{and}B^{T}=B$ Now consider the transpose of $AB-BA$ : $(AB-BA)^{T}=(AB)^{T}-(BA)^{T}$ Using the property $(AB)^{T}=B^{T}A^{T}$ , we get $(AB-BA)^{T}=B^{T}A^{T}-A^{T}B^{T}$ Since $A$ and $B$ are symmetric, $(AB-BA)^{T}=BA-AB$ This can be written as $BA-AB=-(AB-BA)$ So, $(AB-BA)^{T}=-(AB-BA)$ Hence, $AB-BA$ is a skew symmetric matrix. So both statements are true. Correct option: Option C.
questions.explanation_html:
Statement I is true.

A matrix $A$ is called non-singular when its determinant is not zero, that is,

$|A| \ne 0$

For such a matrix, the inverse $A^{-1}$ exists. So Statement I is correct.

Statement II is also true.

Given that $A$ and $B$ are symmetric matrices, we have

$A^{T}=A\text{and}B^{T}=B$

Now consider the transpose of $AB-BA$ :

$(AB-BA)^{T}=(AB)^{T}-(BA)^{T}$

Using the property $(AB)^{T}=B^{T}A^{T}$ , we get

$(AB-BA)^{T}=B^{T}A^{T}-A^{T}B^{T}$

Since $A$ and $B$ are symmetric,

$(AB-BA)^{T}=BA-AB$

This can be written as

$BA-AB=-(AB-BA)$

So,

$(AB-BA)^{T}=-(AB-BA)$

Hence, $AB-BA$ is a skew symmetric matrix.

So both statements are true.

Correct option: Option C.

questions.explanation_text: Given, $A=[\begin{aligned} 1 & tan\frac{\alpha}{2} \\ -tan\frac{\alpha}{2} & 1 \end{aligned}]$ and $AB=I$ $\Rightarrow B=A^{-1}$ Now $A=[\begin{aligned} 1 & tan\frac{\alpha}{2} \\ -tan\frac{\alpha}{2} & 1 \end{aligned}]$ $\begin{aligned} & |A|=[\begin{aligned} 1 & tan\frac{\alpha}{2} \\ -tan\frac{\alpha}{2} & 1 \end{aligned}]=1+an^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}=sec^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2} \\ & adjA=[\begin{aligned} 1 & -tan\frac{\alpha}{2} \\ tan\frac{\alpha}{2} & 1 \end{aligned}] \end{aligned}$ $A^{-1}=\frac{1}{sec^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}}[\begin{aligned} 1 & -tan\frac{\alpha}{2} \\ tan\frac{\alpha}{2} & 1 \end{aligned}]$ $=cos^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}[\begin{aligned} 1 & -tan\frac{\alpha}{2} \\ tan\frac{\alpha}{2} & 1 \end{aligned}]=cos^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}AT$ $B=[cos^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}]AT$
questions.explanation_html:
Given, $A=[\begin{aligned} 1 & tan\frac{\alpha}{2} \\ -tan\frac{\alpha}{2} & 1 \end{aligned}]$ and $AB=I$

$\Rightarrow B=A^{-1}$

Now $A=[\begin{aligned} 1 & tan\frac{\alpha}{2} \\ -tan\frac{\alpha}{2} & 1 \end{aligned}]$

$\begin{aligned} & |A|=[\begin{aligned} 1 & tan\frac{\alpha}{2} \\ -tan\frac{\alpha}{2} & 1 \end{aligned}]=1+an^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}=sec^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2} \\ & adjA=[\begin{aligned} 1 & -tan\frac{\alpha}{2} \\ tan\frac{\alpha}{2} & 1 \end{aligned}] \end{aligned}$

$A^{-1}=\frac{1}{sec^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}}[\begin{aligned} 1 & -tan\frac{\alpha}{2} \\ tan\frac{\alpha}{2} & 1 \end{aligned}]$

$=cos^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}[\begin{aligned} 1 & -tan\frac{\alpha}{2} \\ tan\frac{\alpha}{2} & 1 \end{aligned}]=cos^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}AT$

$B=[cos^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}]AT$

questions.explanation_text: Given, $x^{3}-2x^{2}-9x+18=0$ and $A=|\begin{aligned} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & x & 6 \\ 7 & 8 & 9 \end{aligned}|$ $\begin{aligned} & x^{3}-2x^{2}-9x+18 & =0 \\ \Rightarrow & x^{2}(x-2)-9(x-2) & =0 \\ \Rightarrow & (x^{2}-9)(x-2) & =0 \\ \Rightarrow & (x-3)(x+3)(x-2) & =0 \\ \therefore & x=2,3,-3 \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} A & =|\begin{aligned} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & x & 6 \\ 7 & 8 & 9 \end{aligned}| \\ & =1(9x-48)-2(36-42+3(32-7x) \\ & =9x-48+12+96-21x \\ & =-12x+60 \end{aligned}$ $A$ (when $x=2$ ) $=-12 \times 2+60=36$ $A($ when $x=3)=-12 \times 3+60=24$ $A($ when $x=-3)=-12 \times (-3)+60=96$ More value of $A$ at $x=-3$ is 96.

$\text{Let}A=⎡⎣⎢\begin{aligned} 2 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 3 \end{aligned}⎤⎦⎥$

On applying $R_{1} \rightarrow R_{1}-\frac{5}{2}R_{2},R_{3} \rightarrow R_{3}-\frac{5}{2}R_{2}$ , we get

$⎡⎣⎢\begin{aligned} 1 & 0 & -5/2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1/2 \end{aligned}⎤⎦⎥=⎡⎣⎢\begin{aligned} 1/2 & -5/2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1/2 & -5/2 & 1 \end{aligned}⎤⎦⎥A$

$⎡⎣⎢\begin{aligned} 1 & 0 & -5/2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{aligned}⎤⎦⎥=⎡⎣⎢\begin{aligned} 1/2 & -5/2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -5 & 2 \end{aligned}⎤⎦⎥A$

$R_{1} \rightarrow R_{1}+\frac{5}{2}R_{3},R_{2} \rightarrow R_{2}-R_{3}$ , we get

$⎡⎣⎢\begin{aligned} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{aligned}⎤⎦⎥=⎡⎣⎢\begin{aligned} 3 & -15 & 5 \\ -1 & 6 & -2 \\ 1 & -5 & 2 \end{aligned}⎤⎦⎥A$

Hence, $A^{-1}=⎡⎣⎢\begin{aligned} 3 & -15 & 5 \\ -1 & 6 & -2 \\ 1 & -5 & 2 \end{aligned}⎤⎦⎥$

First, perform the column operation $C_{3} \rightarrow C_{2}+C_{3}$ : $\Delta=|\begin{aligned} a-b & b+c & a+b+c \\ b-a & c+a & a+b+c \\ c-a & a+b & a+b+c \end{aligned}|$ Factor out $(a+b+c)$ , as it's common in the third column: $\Delta=(a+b+c)|\begin{aligned} a-b & b+c & 1 \\ b-a & c+a & 1 \\ c-a & a+b & 1 \end{aligned}|$ Next, apply the row operations $R_{2} \rightarrow R_{2}-R_{1}$ and $R_{3} \rightarrow R_{3}-R_{1}$ : $\Delta=(a+b+c)|\begin{aligned} a-b & b+c & 1 \\ 2b & a-b & 0 \\ c-2a+b & a-c & 0 \end{aligned}|$ Since the last column after the row operations has two zeros, the determinant simplifies to: $\Delta=(a+b+c)(1 \times (2b(a-c)-(a-b)(c-2a+b)))$ Now expand the expression inside the determinant: $=(a+b+c)[2ab-2bc-(ac-2a^{2}+ab-bc+2ab-b^{2})]$ Simplify the terms: $=(a+b+c)[2ab-2bc-ac+2a^{2}-ab+bc-2ab+b^{2}]$ Resulting in: $=(a+b+c)[2a^{2}-ac-ab-bc+b^{2}]$

To find the value of the determinant $\Delta=|\begin{aligned} a-b & b+c & a \\ b-a & c+a & b \\ c-a & a+b & c \end{aligned}|$ , we can proceed with column and row operations to simplify it.

First, perform the column operation $C_{3} \rightarrow C_{2}+C_{3}$ :

$\Delta=|\begin{aligned} a-b & b+c & a+b+c \\ b-a & c+a & a+b+c \\ c-a & a+b & a+b+c \end{aligned}|$

Factor out $(a+b+c)$ , as it's common in the third column:

$\Delta=(a+b+c)|\begin{aligned} a-b & b+c & 1 \\ b-a & c+a & 1 \\ c-a & a+b & 1 \end{aligned}|$

Next, apply the row operations $R_{2} \rightarrow R_{2}-R_{1}$ and $R_{3} \rightarrow R_{3}-R_{1}$ :

$\Delta=(a+b+c)|\begin{aligned} a-b & b+c & 1 \\ 2b & a-b & 0 \\ c-2a+b & a-c & 0 \end{aligned}|$

Since the last column after the row operations has two zeros, the determinant simplifies to:

$\Delta=(a+b+c)(1 \times (2b(a-c)-(a-b)(c-2a+b)))$

Now expand the expression inside the determinant:

$=(a+b+c)[2ab-2bc-(ac-2a^{2}+ab-bc+2ab-b^{2})]$

Simplify the terms:

$=(a+b+c)[2ab-2bc-ac+2a^{2}-ab+bc-2ab+b^{2}]$

Resulting in:

$=(a+b+c)[2a^{2}-ac-ab-bc+b^{2}]$

Thus, the inverse is: $\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{aligned}]$ Substitute the inverse into the expression for $[\begin{aligned} x \\ y \end{aligned}]$ : $[\begin{aligned} x \\ y \end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{aligned}][\begin{aligned} 2 \\ 4 \end{aligned}]$ Calculate the matrix product: $\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned} (1)(2)+(-1)(4) \\ (1)(2)+(1)(4) \end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned} 2-4 \\ 2+4 \end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned} -2 \\ 6 \end{aligned}]$ This simplifies to: $[\begin{aligned} x \\ y \end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned} -1 \\ 3 \end{aligned}]$ Therefore, the values of $x$ and $y$ are $x=-1$ and $y=3$ .

To find the values of $x$ and $y$ , we start with the matrix equation:

$[\begin{aligned} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{aligned}][\begin{aligned} x \\ y \end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned} 2 \\ 4 \end{aligned}]$

We can solve for the vector $[\begin{aligned} x \\ y \end{aligned}]$ using the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$[\begin{aligned} x \\ y \end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{aligned}]^{-1}[\begin{aligned} 2 \\ 4 \end{aligned}]$

The inverse of the matrix $[\begin{aligned} a & b \\ c & d \end{aligned}]$ is given by:

$[\begin{aligned} a & b \\ c & d \end{aligned}]^{-1}=\frac{1}{ad-bc}[\begin{aligned} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{aligned}]$

For our matrix $[\begin{aligned} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{aligned}]$ , the determinant $ad-bc=(1)(1)-(1)(-1)=2$ .

Thus, the inverse is:

$\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{aligned}]$

Substitute the inverse into the expression for $[\begin{aligned} x \\ y \end{aligned}]$ :

$[\begin{aligned} x \\ y \end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{aligned}][\begin{aligned} 2 \\ 4 \end{aligned}]$

Calculate the matrix product:

$\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned} (1)(2)+(-1)(4) \\ (1)(2)+(1)(4) \end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned} 2-4 \\ 2+4 \end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned} -2 \\ 6 \end{aligned}]$

This simplifies to:

$[\begin{aligned} x \\ y \end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned} -1 \\ 3 \end{aligned}]$

Therefore, the values of $x$ and $y$ are $x=-1$ and $y=3$ .

Given the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned} cos\alpha & sin\alpha \\ -sin\alpha & cos\alpha \end{aligned}]$ , we need to calculate the product $AA^{'}$ , where $A^{'}$ is the transpose of matrix $A$ .

The transpose of $A$ , denoted $A^{'}$ , is:

$A^{'}=[\begin{aligned} cos\alpha & -sin\alpha \\ sin\alpha & cos\alpha \end{aligned}]$

Now, we calculate the product $AA^{'}$ :

$AA^{'}=[\begin{aligned} cos\alpha & sin\alpha \\ -sin\alpha & cos\alpha \end{aligned}][\begin{aligned} cos\alpha & -sin\alpha \\ sin\alpha & cos\alpha \end{aligned}]$

Performing the matrix multiplication, we have:

$AA^{'}=[\begin{aligned} (cos\alpha)(cos\alpha)+(sin\alpha)(sin\alpha) & (cos\alpha)(-sin\alpha)+(sin\alpha)(cos\alpha) \\ (-sin\alpha)(cos\alpha)+(cos\alpha)(sin\alpha) & (-sin\alpha)(-sin\alpha)+(cos\alpha)(cos\alpha) \end{aligned}]$

Calculating each element:

Top left: $cos^{2}\alpha+sin^{2}\alpha=1$ (using the Pythagorean identity)

Top right: $-cos\alpha sin\alpha+sin\alpha cos\alpha=0$

Bottom left: $-sin\alpha cos\alpha+cos\alpha sin\alpha=0$

Bottom right: $sin^{2}\alpha+cos^{2}\alpha=1$ (using the Pythagorean identity)

Thus, the product is:

$AA^{'}=[\begin{aligned} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{aligned}]$

This is the identity matrix $I$ . Hence,

$AA^{'}=I$
